title: How the Church Took Over the Empire

keyTerms.d: The sociologist Rodney Stark’s way of defusing the apparent miracle in the numbers: assume the church grew at a constant compound rate, anchor it to a starting figure and an endpoint historians roughly accept, and see what the exponential curve produces. Begin with about a thousand Christians in the year 40 and let the movement grow at 40 per cent per decade — a little under three and a half per cent a year — and you reach something over a tenth of a sixty-million empire by 300. Forty per cent a decade is not a stampede; it is what you get if, over a decade, roughly two or three believers together bring in one new person — no mass conversions, no coercion. Stark said plainly it is a model, not a census; every figure in every book is an estimate built from fragments.

The best evidence that the church was growing comes not from Christians, who had every reason to advertise their success, but from officials and critics who found the movement irritating, contemptible, or alarming — and described it anyway. Pliny the Younger (c. 112) reports the “contagion of this superstition” spreading through cities, villages, and countryside; Lucian of Samosata (c. 165), who thought Christians credulous fools, describes their organised, costly support for a jailed leader. The contempt is what makes the testimony valuable: a hostile source is not building a case for the church when it confirms the church was organised, generous, and spreading.

The standard sceptical reply, stated at its strongest because part of it is simply accurate: the real cause of Christianity’s success is not the mechanisms of the movement but a single political event. In 312 Constantine won at the Milvian Bridge and credited the Christian God; in 313 the settlement loosely called the Edict of Milan ended persecution; imperial patronage followed; and in 380 Theodosius made Nicene Christianity official, with the coercive power of the state behind it. On this telling, Christianity did not win the Roman world — it was handed it. The reply is not to deny it but to date it: it explains the fourth century, and reverses cause and effect for the stretch before 312.

The decisive fact about timing. The state’s own attempts to destroy the church had already failed with the full machinery of empire engaged — Decius’s universal sacrifice order of 250, Valerian’s edicts of 257 and 258, and Diocletian’s persecution from 303 were all spent, and the last was formally abandoned by Galerius in the edict of toleration of April 311: a full year before the Milvian Bridge (though Maximinus Daia soon renewed it in the eastern provinces he ruled until his defeat in 313). The state conceded first. By the time Constantine acted, the church already reached into the army and the palace and numbered in the millions.

Stark’s most durable contribution, sociological rather than statistical: new religious movements grow overwhelmingly along existing relationships — family, household, trade, friendship — rather than through public preaching to strangers. The book of Acts shows exactly this, converting whole households at a stroke (Cornelius, Lydia, the Philippian jailer, Crispus) alongside the public preaching it also records. It is an unglamorous mechanism, and it is precisely what produces the steady compounding the arithmetic describes: not a wave, but a web, thickening decade by decade — the faith spreading the way trust spreads, one relationship at a time.

keyTerms.t: A wider door than anyone else offered
keyTerms.d: Leaving an unwanted newborn outdoors to die or be taken was legal and unremarkable in the Greco-Roman world; Christian texts forbid it from their earliest layer (the Didache bans it in the same breath as murder; the Epistle to Diognetus singles out Christians who “do not destroy their offspring”). The same communities admitted, without a bar of status, the categories the surrounding cults ranked and rationed — slaves, the poor, women, and non-Greeks. The claim must be kept bounded: careful specialists such as Lynn Cohick show Greco-Roman women had wider scope than the old caricature allowed, so the defensible point is the narrower, sturdier one — the communities were unusually mixed, and membership was not priced by rank.

The load-bearing honest limit, kept distinct from everything else. The rapid, illegal, person-to-person spread of the church shows that the faith was profoundly attractive and that its people were utterly convinced — convinced enough to nurse plague victims at the cost of their lives and to keep confessing the name when a pinch of incense would have bought their safety. But it is not, by itself, proof that the gospel is true, and the argument does not offer it as one: movements can spread quickly and still be mistaken; popularity is not a truth-detector. Stark himself notes his assumed rate is close to the twentieth-century growth of the Latter-day Saints, so a curve of this shape is not unique to Christianity. The case that Jesus actually rose rests on different evidence — the early eyewitness creed of 1 Corinthians 15:3–7 — made elsewhere in the Library.

The sharpest testimony to what had driven the growth, from the one man with the most reason to deny it — and its date must be stated, not blurred, because it is not evidence from the illegal centuries. It comes fifty years after Constantine. In 362 the emperor Julian, raised Christian and the only emperor after Constantine to abandon the faith, set out to restore the old gods, and diagnosed that the Christians were winning because they out-behaved the pagans: when the pagan priesthood neglected the poor, “the impious Galilaeans” devoted themselves to philanthropy and so “led very many into atheism,” and his remedy was to urge his own priests to copy the charity he had set out to defeat. The quotation is grounded only in the undisputed Fragment of a Letter to a Priest; the more famous Letter to Arsacius, whose genuineness Van Nuffelen has challenged, is not relied on. Julian witnesses what the church’s enemy judged he had to beat — not why it grew in the second and third centuries.

derive.q: Begin with about a thousand Christians in the year 40 and grow the movement at 40 per cent per decade — two or three believers together bringing in one new person over a decade. To reach a tenth of the empire by 300 you need…?
derive.ans: nothing miraculous, forced, or unusual — only steady, ordinary, person-to-person growth kept up a very long time
derive.why: The force of the model is what it rules out. Forty per cent a decade is not a stampede; it is what you get if, over a decade, roughly two or three believers together bring in one new person. There is no need for mass conversions or coercion — neither of which existed in this period anyway. The numbers do not require anything miraculous, forced, or even unusual; they require only steady, ordinary, person-to-person growth, kept up for a very long time.

derive.q: Pliny describes a spreading movement around 112; Lucian its organised charity around 165; Cornelius’s relief roll lists 1,500 dependants in 251 — all before any emperor favoured the faith. So the Constantine story…?
derive.ans: explains the wrong stretch of the curve — for the period before 312 it reverses cause and effect
derive.why: The objection explains the wrong stretch of the curve, and three facts sit entirely outside the window the state can cover. Pliny’s letter and Lucian’s satire describe a spreading, organised movement in the second century, when no emperor favoured it. Cornelius’s relief roll is an administrative document from an illegal church in 251. The Constantine story does not explain the growth before 312 — for that stretch it reverses cause and effect.

derive.q: Decius (250), Valerian (257–58) and Diocletian (303) all tried to destroy the church with the full machinery of empire, and all were spent; Galerius conceded toleration in April 311, a year before the Milvian Bridge. So the first mover was…?
derive.ans: the state — it conceded first; Constantine recognised a movement already too big to suppress, he did not create it
derive.why: This is decisive: the state’s own attempts to destroy the church had already failed with the full machinery of empire engaged, and the last was formally abandoned by Galerius in the edict of toleration of April 311 — a full year before the Milvian Bridge. The state conceded first. By the time Constantine acted, the church already reached into the army and the palace and numbered in the millions; his patronage recognised and accelerated a movement already too big to suppress.

derive.q: The spread shows the movement was profoundly attractive and its people utterly convinced — convinced enough to nurse the dying and refuse a pinch of incense that would buy their safety. Does that establish that the gospel is true?
derive.ans: no — popularity is not a truth-detector; the case that Jesus rose rests on the resurrection evidence, made elsewhere
derive.why: It is not, by itself, proof that the gospel is true, and this essay does not offer it as one. Movements can spread quickly and still be mistaken; popularity is not a truth-detector. The case that Jesus actually rose from the dead rests on different evidence — above all the eyewitness testimony behind the early creed Paul hands on in 1 Corinthians 15:3–7. What the growth does do is exactly what you would expect if that resurrection claim were true and its first witnesses sincere.

derive.q: Julian (362) is fifty years after Constantine, far too late to explain the second- and third-century growth. So the most reason-to-deny-it witness is a witness to…?
derive.ans: what the church’s fiercest opponent, with an empire at his disposal, judged he had to copy — its charity
derive.why: Julian is not a witness to why the church grew in the second and third centuries — he is far too late for that, and it must not be pretended otherwise. But he is a witness to something worth having: an emperor holding the whole apparatus of the state, and using it against the church, judged that the thing he had to defeat was Christian charity, and set out to copy it. When your fiercest opponent, with an empire at his disposal, sets out to imitate you, he has told you where the movement’s real strength lay.

honestState.p1: What this argument establishes is bounded, and the track keeps it honest throughout. It establishes two things, and no more: that the popular “Constantine did it” story is false as an account of the period that matters — the church became too large to suppress before the state had any part in it — and that the growth was real and costly, run on care of the sick, refusal to expose infants, mutual aid, and conversion along household networks, with the charity at its heart attested even by hostile witnesses. The numbers themselves stay a range: estimates for AD 300 run from Ehrman’s two and a half or three million to Stark’s six-point-three million, a model and not a census. What the argument does not establish is that Christianity is true; growth never shows that.
honestState.fairness: The scope is kept honest by naming the critics who keep it so. Bart Ehrman puts the year-300 figure at less than half Stark’s and warns the constant rate cannot simply be extended, since running it to 400 yields more Christians than the empire had inhabitants. Keith Hopkins, often cited as independent confirmation, is not — he adopts Stark’s endpoints and arithmetic, so he corroborates the method, not the conclusion. Ramsay MacMullen, the leading dissenting historian, argues conversion turned less on charity than on displays of power (healings and exorcisms); his is a rival account of the mechanism, answered here only in part, and no help to the Constantine objection, since whatever exorcism was, it was not imperial power. Lynn Cohick keeps the “wider door” claim bounded. Stark’s most contested element — that nursing was demographically consequential — rests on modern estimates applied to diseases we cannot securely identify, and is weighed as an argument, not a demonstrated result.
honestState.verdict: So the honest takeaway is not a boast but a recognition. A tiny, powerless, illegal movement outlasted the empire that tried to kill it — not by force, which in those centuries it never had, but by costly behaviour its enemies could see and its first opponents set out to copy. The claim that Christianity owes its position to the state is false for the period that matters: the state conceded first, and Constantine recognised a movement already too big to suppress. That is astonishing enough without inflating it — and it is deliberately not the claim that the faith is true. The behaviours that carried the church across the empire were what Jesus had told his followers to do, done at cost by people who mostly left no names, because they believed he had been raised. The growth is exactly what you would expect if that resurrection claim were true; it is not a substitute for the argument that it is, which rests on the resurrection and is made elsewhere in the Library.

order: The church grew from a few hundred to a substantial minority of the empire within three centuries, while the faith was illegal and carried no political advantage — and the charity at the heart of that growth is attested even by hostile witnesses.

This growth is far better explained by the movement’s own resources — its care of strangers, its networks, the conviction behind it — than by imperial power, which arrived only after the church was already too large to suppress.

Therefore the claim that Christianity owes its position to the state is false for the period that matters — though this establishes that the growth was real and unassisted by the state, not that the faith is true.

the charity at the heart of the growth is attested even by hostile witnesses — Pliny, Lucian, Cornelius’s relief roll
the church was already too large to suppress before Constantine acted — the state conceded first in 311
the growth ran on costly behaviour — care of the sick, refusal to expose infants, mutual aid, household networks

cards.q: State Premise 1 — and its precision check.
cards.a: The church grew from a few hundred to a substantial minority of the empire within three centuries, while the faith was illegal and carried no political advantage — and the charity at the heart of that growth is attested even by hostile witnesses. Precision: the claim is about the shape of the growth, not a census. Nobody counted, so every figure is an estimate built from fragments; what is not in dispute is a standing start and steep, sustained growth, achieved while the faith was illegal.

cards.q: State Premise 2 — and its precision check.
cards.a: This growth is far better explained by the movement’s own resources — care of strangers, networks, the conviction behind it — than by imperial power, which arrived only after the church was already too large to suppress. Precision: an inference to the best explanation, deliberately bounded. No single cause explains three centuries across a whole empire, and none of these mechanisms is unique in kind — the claim is about their combination and cost.

cards.q: What does the conclusion reach — and what does it NOT reach?
cards.a: It reaches that the claim Christianity owes its position to the state is false for the period that matters — the church was already too large to suppress before 312. It does NOT reach that the faith is true; growth never shows that. The argument answers the “Constantine did it” story for the stretch before 312, and it stops there.

cards.q: Why does the Constantine objection explain “the wrong stretch of the curve”?
cards.a: Concede the fourth century entirely: after 312 everything is entangled with state power and the majority was reached under that thumb, so the AD 400 majority is not evidence of persuasive force. But Pliny, Lucian and Cornelius all predate Constantine, and two persecutions had already failed. By the time Constantine acted the church already numbered in the millions; his patronage recognised a movement already too big to suppress — for the stretch before 312 the objection reverses cause and effect.

cards.q: Name the three pre-Constantinian witnesses and why each carries weight.
cards.a: Pliny (c. 112), a Roman governor alarmed that the “superstition” had spread through cities and countryside, every age and rank and both sexes — a private request for guidance, not a victory bulletin. Lucian (c. 165), a hostile satirist whose contempt is what makes his account of their organised, costly charity valuable. Cornelius of Rome (251), whose relief roll of 46 presbyters and over 1,500 dependants is an internal administrative record — “a relief roll, not a boast.” Two are hostile, one is internal, and all three predate any imperial favour.

cards.q: Why does Galerius’s edict of 311 matter to the timing of the argument?
cards.a: Because it shows the state conceded first. Decius’s order of 250, Valerian’s edicts of 257–58 and Diocletian’s persecution from 303 were all spent, and the last was formally abandoned by Galerius in the edict of toleration of April 311 — a full year before the Milvian Bridge of 312. So Constantine did not create the movement; the state gave up fighting one that had already grown while completely illegal.

cards.q: “It grew fast, so it must be true.” What is the reply — and why is this the one that matters most?
cards.a: This one cuts against us, and we grant it in our own voice: growth is not truth. People risk much for beliefs that turn out false, and fast growth is not unique to Christianity — Stark observed his rate is close to the twentieth-century growth of the Latter-day Saints, a curve of the same shape. The rise shows the movement was compelling and costly to join; whether its central claim is true rests on the resurrection, argued elsewhere. The argument’s job is the narrower one: to refute the claim that the state did it.

cards.q: Why is Stark’s figure “a model, not a census,” and does the case rest on it?
cards.a: There was never any count of Christians in the empire; every figure is an estimate built from fragments, and Stark said his table is a model generated from an assumed constant rate. It cannot even be extended past the mid-fourth century without exceeding the empire’s population. That is why the honest answer is a range — roughly 2.5 to 6.3 million by 300 — and why the case does not rest on the numbers at all, but on the datable, hostile, pre-Constantinian evidence that a large organised movement already existed.

cards.q: Why is Keith Hopkins NOT independent confirmation of the high figure?
cards.a: Because he takes Stark’s arithmetic as his starting point — he adopts Stark’s endpoints and rate rather than reaching an independent estimate, and his contribution is to probe what such totals imply about community size and structure. He is therefore corroboration of Stark’s method, not of his conclusion, so he cannot be cited as an independent second voice for the numbers.

cards.q: Care of the sick during the plagues — what it shows, and the honest limit.
cards.a: The empire was twice gutted by epidemics with no capacity for mass nursing, and Dionysius of Alexandria describes Christians staying with the dying and perishing in numbers while frightened neighbours abandoned their own. The behaviour is well attested and is the sort of thing that changes how a neighbour thinks. Honest limit: Stark’s further claim — that this was demographically consequential — rests on modern estimates applied to diseases we cannot securely identify, so it is a plausible argument rather than a proven result.

cards.q: The “wider door” — state the bounded claim, not the overstatement.
cards.a: Christian texts forbid exposing newborns from their earliest layer, and the communities admitted slaves, the poor, women and non-Greeks without a bar of status, on the same terms. But the point is easy to overstate: careful specialists such as Lynn Cohick show Greco-Roman women had wider social and economic scope than the old caricature allowed. So the defensible claim is the narrower, sturdier one — the communities were unusually mixed, and membership was not priced by rank.

cards.q: The emperor Julian (AD 362) — what does he witness, and what does he NOT?
cards.a: He does NOT witness why the church grew in the second and third centuries — he is fifty years after Constantine, far too late for that, and it must not be pretended otherwise. He witnesses that an emperor holding the whole apparatus of the state, trying to restore paganism, judged Christian charity the thing he had to beat and urged his own priests to copy it (the undisputed Fragment of a Letter to a Priest; the more famous Letter to Arsacius is disputed and not relied on).

obj.q: Christianity only took over because Constantine made it the state religion. In 312 he won at the Milvian Bridge and credited the Christian God; patronage followed, and in 380 Theodosius made Nicene Christianity official with the coercive power of the state behind it. It didn’t win the argument; it won the palace — it was handed the Roman world from the top.
obj.model: The concession owed here is substantial, and we grant it: everything after 312 is entangled with state power, and the church’s growth after 380 with the legal suppression of rival worship. The steepest part of the curve in raw numbers is the fourth century, and anyone who points to the Christian majority of AD 400 as proof of the gospel’s persuasive force is trading on a period when the state’s thumb was on the scale. But the objection explains the wrong stretch of the curve. Pliny describes a spreading movement around 112, Lucian its organised charity around 165, and Cornelius’s relief roll of 251 lists over 1,500 dependants in a single illegal church — all before any emperor favoured it. And this is decisive: the state’s own attempts to destroy the church had already failed with the full machinery of empire engaged, the last formally abandoned by Galerius in April 311, a full year before the Milvian Bridge. The state conceded first. By the time Constantine acted the church already reached into the army and the palace and numbered in the millions; his patronage recognised and accelerated a movement already too big to suppress. So “Constantine did it” is false for the period that matters — for the growth before 312 it reverses cause and effect.

obj.q: A movement that spreads this quickly, against this much resistance, must have had the truth on its side — why else would people risk everything for it? The sheer growth is itself the evidence that Christianity is true.
obj.model: This one cuts against us, and we grant it: growth is not truth. People risk much for beliefs that turn out false, and fast growth is not unique to Christianity — Stark observed that his assumed rate is close to the documented twentieth-century growth of the Latter-day Saints, an exponential curve of the same shape, which is a plausibility check on a rate already chosen, not an input to it. So the honest verdict is bounded: the rise of the church shows the movement was profoundly attractive and that its people were utterly convinced — convinced enough to nurse plague victims at the cost of their lives and to keep confessing the name when a pinch of incense would have bought their safety. It does not show that the movement’s central claims are true. The case that Jesus actually rose from the dead rests on different evidence — above all the early eyewitness creed in 1 Corinthians 15:3–7 — and is made elsewhere in the Library. The growth is exactly what you would expect if that claim were true, not a substitute for the argument that it is.

obj.q: The leading dissenting historian, Ramsay MacMullen, argued that conversion in this period turned less on charity than on public demonstrations of power — healings and exorcisms a pagan could read as a straight contest between gods. Your charity story is the wrong mechanism.
obj.model: His is a serious rival account of the mechanism — one that discounts charity in favour of displays of power — and it is answered here only in part. Two things keep it from unseating the argument. First, the two accounts are not exclusive, because the charity is independently attested — by Lucian’s sneer, by Cornelius’s relief roll, and by Dionysius — whatever weight one gives the exorcisms. Second, and decisively for the point in dispute, MacMullen’s account is no help to the Constantine objection at all: whatever exorcism was, it was not imperial power. So even if power-displays did more of the work than charity, the state still did not drive the growth before 312 — which is exactly the claim this argument lands.

obj.q: The six-million figure is a model built on an assumed growth rate, not a census. Nobody counted, so you can make it say whatever you assume — the numbers are just an apologist’s guess.
obj.model: True, and the track says so first. There was never any count of Christians in the empire, and every figure in every book is an estimate built from fragments; Stark’s table is explicitly a model generated from an assumed constant rate, and it cannot even be extended past the mid-fourth century without exceeding the empire’s population. The scholarly agreement is also thinner than it can look: Keith Hopkins, often cited as independent confirmation, is not — he takes Stark’s arithmetic as his starting point. That is exactly why the honest answer is a range — roughly two and a half to six million by 300, unevenly spread and concentrated in the cities — and why the case does not rest on the numbers at all, but on the datable, hostile, pre-Constantinian evidence that a large, organised movement already existed. The shape — a standing start and steep, sustained growth, achieved while the faith was illegal — is not in dispute, and it is astonishing enough without inflating it.

unseen.q: Your own best evidence sinks you. Dionysius says the Christians who nursed the dying perished in numbers as a result. So if anything, plague should have thinned the Christians faster than the pagans who fled — the care-for-the-sick mechanism is self-defeating, and it cannot have fuelled the growth at all.
unseen.model: The behaviour is what matters, and it is well attested; the demographic claim built on top of it is exactly the part the track marks as contested, not load-bearing. Stark’s much-quoted move is that costly nursing was not merely admirable but demographically consequential: even elementary nursing can cut mortality sharply, so tended communities lost fewer of their own and won the loyalty of the strangers they had nursed — a net effect that holds even though some carers died. But that model rests on modern estimates applied to diseases we cannot securely identify, and Dionysius’s own report that the carers died illustrates the tension, so it should be weighed as a plausible argument rather than a demonstrated result. Crucially, the argument does not depend on it. What is securely attested is the conduct — Christians staying with the dying while frightened neighbours abandoned their own — and it is the sort of thing that changes how a neighbour thinks. Even if the differential-mortality mechanism is set aside entirely, the case still stands on the datable, hostile, pre-Constantinian evidence of a large organised movement; and the costly behaviour itself is what the church’s own enemies — Lucian, and later Julian — could see and judged they had to reckon with.
